A release has two steps: upload every new asset under a versioned name (for example, `app.3f9c2.js`), then switch the manifest to point at those names.

The upload comes first because the manifest switch is what makes the new version live. Once a browser fetches the new manifest, it immediately requests the files it names. If those files aren't uploaded yet, the browser gets 404s and loads a broken page. Uploading first means every name in the manifest already exists by the time anyone can see it. Uploading is also safe to do early: nothing references the new names until the switch, and because the names are versioned, they don't overwrite anything that's currently in use.

We keep the old assets because the switch doesn't reach everyone at once. A browser that loaded the previous manifest before the switch will keep requesting the old versioned files, whether for lazy-loaded chunks, later navigation, or a tab left open. If we deleted those files, those users would hit missing assets in the middle of a session. Keeping them means every manifest a browser might hold, old or new, still points at files that exist.

A release has two steps: upload every new asset under a versioned name (e.g. `app.3f9c.js`), then switch the manifest to point at those names. The manifest is the only thing that decides which assets a page loads, so the switch is the moment the release goes live.

**Why the upload comes first:** once the manifest is switched, any browser that fetches it will immediately request the new names. If those files weren't already uploaded, those requests would fail and users would get a broken page. Uploading first means every name the new manifest references already exists when it goes live. Because the new files have new names, uploading them can't affect anyone still on the old manifest.

**Why we keep the old assets:** browsers that fetched the previous manifest before the switch will keep requesting the old names, for example when lazy-loading a chunk or loading the next page. If we deleted the old files at switch time, those requests would fail mid-session. Leaving the old assets in place lets those browsers finish on the old version while new visitors get the new one.
